title: Four levels of reading
hookLine: the plain meaning, the hint, the teaching and the secret: pardes

cards: An orchard. In the Song of Songs, the lover says, in the King James words, "Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits." The Hebrew word for orchard there is pardes.
Much later, Jewish readers turned that same word into a map for reading scripture. Its four consonants, P, R, D, S, became the first letters of four ways into a text.
You can walk in at the gate and see the trees, or go deeper and find what's growing underneath. Today we take the walk, and learn which gate comes first.

teach.b: Here are the four. P is peshat: the plain meaning, what the words say in their own setting. R is remez: the hint, pointed to by a detail, a number, a strange word choice.

D is derash: the teaching drawn out by searching the text, the way the rabbis of the midrash read it, finding lessons and stories in its gaps. And S is sod: the secret, the hidden meaning the mystics looked for.
Take the Song of Songs. Its peshat is a love poem between two people. Its derash, in rabbinic tradition, is the love between God and the people of Israel.
Both readings live side by side. But there's an order.

teach.h: A VERSE KEEPS ITS PLAIN MEANING.
teach.b: The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, records a short rule: a verse does not depart from its plain meaning.
You can read deeper, but you can't read past the words as if they weren't there.
The commentator Rashi, in his note on Genesis 3:8, says he has come only for the plain sense of the verse, and for the midrash that helps settle its words.
The same rule works far from any scroll: a message or a friend's sentence can be read for hidden meanings before anyone has read what it actually says.
Before you hunt for the hint, the teaching or the secret, ask the plain question first: what do these words say?

how: Jewish Bibles are studied with commentaries printed around the text, such as Rashi, which give the plain meaning and rabbinic teachings side by side, and students learn to say which kind of reading they are offering.

o: a secret meaning that only the mystics can find

games.q: the four letters of pardes — tap the pairs.

s: pardes is a Hebrew word for orchard
it appears in the Song of Songs: an orchard of pomegranates.
the deeper readings replace the plain meaning
the Talmud says a verse does not depart from its plain meaning.
the Song of Songs can only be read one way

games.q: you're reading a verse for the first time. which of the four ways do you start with?
games.why: plain meaning first. the Talmud's rule: a verse does not depart from its plain meaning.

practice: Take the last words of the Hebrew Bible, ve-ya'al, and let him go up, and stay first with the plain meaning: Cyrus, king of Persia, tells the exiles they may go up to Jerusalem and rebuild.

Only then let a second reading come, what going up might mean in your own life, and keep the two side by side without letting the second erase the first. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition for clear eyes when you read.

wordCard.voice: Peshat. The plain meaning of a verse, the first of the four ways into the orchard: peshat, remez, derash, sod. Today's word.
